title: Marpa
hookLine: the farmer-translator who walked to India three times for the teachings

cards: He wasn't a monk. He had a wife, a farm, fields to watch and a temper to match, and he liked his beer, the stories say. And Tibetans remember him with deep honor.
His name was Marpa, known as Marpa the Translator. Tradition says he made the trip from Tibet over the Himalaya to India three times, on foot, to find teachers and bring their words home.

teach.b: The teachings weren't free, and the road was dangerous: mountain passes, fevers in the hot plains below, robbers. In the stories, Marpa turned what he owned into gold to offer his teachers, and walked.
In India he found Naropa, yesterday's scholar, now a master himself, and studied with him and others.

He learned the language well enough to carry not only texts but their meaning, which yesterday's story says is the hard part. Each time, he came back to Tibet and worked: translating, teaching, farming.
He didn't shave his head or enter a monastery.

He showed that a householder could carry a lineage, with a family and a farm around him. Why go again? Tradition gives more than one reason: to fill gaps, to receive teachings he'd missed, to see his teacher once more.

Marpa had enough to be a respected teacher at home, and still went back, because enough wasn't the point. The Kagyu tradition remembers him as the link between Naropa in India and the Tibetan students who came after.
One of them, Milarepa, fills the next several days, and Marpa will turn out to be a fierce and strange teacher.
His journeys leave a plain question: what would you walk a long way for? Not buy, not download. Walk for, come back with, and walk for again.

how: In the Kagyu school, Marpa is honored as the translator who brought Naropa's teachings to Tibet, and his image, often shown as a stocky layman rather than a monk, appears in Kagyu lineage paintings and prayers.

games.q: you're Marpa, back home, respected as a teacher and translator. you know there are teachings you missed in India. what do you do?
o: send a letter asking for the texts.
games.why: tradition says Marpa went back to India again, three journeys in all, for what he had missed.

practice: Ask quietly what is worth real effort to you, a skill, a relationship, a question, a practice, and let one thing come.
Picture the first stretch of the road toward it, one small, concrete step, and see yourself taking it as the breath carries you on.

wordCard.voice: Marpa. The farmer and householder who, tradition says, walked to India three times and carried the teaching home as a translator. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: three journeys. Enough was never the point. Nine hundred seventy-one days, and counting.
